justifications.functional_suitability: All four functional requirements map to elements: Patient & Scheduling Service (registration, scheduling), EMR Service with Audit Interceptor, Billing & Claims Service with Claims Engine. Gaps: clash-check logic is not explicit, and the Scheduling Engine does not specify resource conflict detection.
justifications.performance_efficiency: Redis Enterprise and Local EMR Cache Manager (read-through/write-behind), PgBouncer pooling, read replicas, async Kafka audit and Outbox Dispatcher support the <1s P95 EMR target. Gaps: no explicit autoscaling or latency budget, and the cache is not tied to the 1s figure.
justifications.compatibility: Integration Service with FHIR Adapter, Apache Camel, and API Gateway FHIR Request Validator addresses HL7 FHIR for lab and imaging. OIDC/SAML IdP and clearinghouse REST/SFTP are covered. Gaps: the FHIR Gateway is only a context-level component, and the Level 3 Integration Service mixes in unrelated elements.
justifications.usability: A single SPA/Mobile Client serves all five user groups, with EMR Workspace, Notification & Alert UI, RBAC Context Provider and Offline Sync Engine. Gaps: no role-specific interfaces for receptionist, billing or patient, and no accessibility or UX mechanisms.
justifications.reliability: Active-active PostgreSQL, etcd/Raft fencing, Kubernetes Operator, WAL Archiver, Redis CRDT Sync, Resilience & Policy Engine circuit breaking, DLQ Manager and Outbox Dispatcher address 99.99%. Gaps: the multi-region failover design is unclear and the primary/replica description conflicts with active-active.
justifications.security: IdP MFA via OIDC, JWT Validation Plugin, mTLS Service Mesh, AES-256 PostgreSQL and Redis, RBAC Context Provider, immutable Audit Interceptor, Audit & Compliance Service with S3 WORM Object Lock, Report Generator & Redactor, and Cache Purge Controller for GDPR cover the brief thoroughly.
justifications.maintainability: Clear service decomposition with separate Patient & Scheduling, EMR, Billing, Integration and Audit containers. A service mesh and API Gateway decouple concerns, and components are well scoped. Gaps: mixed technology options (Java/Node, Python/Go) and inconsistent L3 diagrams embedding containers and external systems as components.
justifications.portability: Kubernetes, the CloudNativePG operator, Istio, and the Redis hybrid VPN tunnel manager fit on-prem plus eu-central-1. Containerized open technologies limit lock-in. Gaps: AWS S3 Object Lock is a specific dependency and no explicit deployment or IaC definition exists.

sensitivity_points: Cache hit ratio determines P95 latency
Write-behind may serve stale EMR data
tradeoffs: Audit and mTLS hops add latency
PERF-01.justification: Read-through Redis cache, pooling and read replicas support sub-second loads. However, no explicit autoscaling, load figures or freshness guarantees are given, and write-behind risks stale data, so the P95 target is unproven.

sensitivity_points: No inbound lab-to-EMR path is modeled
tradeoffs: Async ingestion vs. EMR visibility delay
Shared database couples ingestion and EMR reads
PERF-02.justification: Camel/Spring Integration with a DLQ can handle bursts, and replicas isolate reads. But the flow into the EMR is not modeled, there is no ingest queue or scaling, and the shared database is a contention risk.

sensitivity_points: Cross-region replication is asynchronous, so data loss is possible
No global traffic failover mechanism is shown
tradeoffs: Async replication performance vs. zero data loss
AVAIL-01.justification: A hybrid topology, Raft failover and Redis CRDTs help. But the cross-region replica is asynchronous, which conflicts with no data loss, and DNS/global load balancing for the 1-minute switchover is missing.

sensitivity_points: Idempotency of claim submission to the clearinghouse
tradeoffs: Outbox gives reliability at the cost of delivery latency
AVAIL-02.justification: Outbox pattern, Raft leader election and a synchronous on-prem replica support safe retry and fast failover. No explicit idempotency keys or deduplication against the clearinghouse are shown, so duplicates remain a risk.

sensitivity_points: Claims Engine may be coupled to the clearinghouse protocol
tradeoffs: Service-level isolation vs. no dedicated adapter layer
MOD-01.justification: Claims are isolated in Billing & Claims Service, so the EMR is unaffected. The change likely touches the Claims Engine, and there is no explicit clearinghouse adapter interface, but it is still confined to one container.

sensitivity_points: Audit capture is not tied to the demographic fields
tradeoffs: Shared database eases consistency but couples changes
Generic audit hashing reduces change but weakens field-level audit
MOD-02.justification: The change touches the UI, patient service, database schema and possibly audit rules, which is about three or more components. No schema-migration or field-level audit configuration is described, so the one-sprint target is a risk.

sensitivity_points: MFA is enforced only at the IdP
Failed-login events are not routed to the Audit Service
tradeoffs: External IdP delegation vs. dependence on the vendor
SEC-01.justification: The IdP enforces MFA and the gateway validates JWTs, so no access without the second factor is plausible. But failed login attempts reach the audit and alerting pipeline only implicitly, so the 1-minute alert is not demonstrated.

sensitivity_points: Async audit dispatch may drop events
Policy check on treating relationship is not explicit
tradeoffs: Async auditing preserves latency but risks gaps
SEC-02.justification: Audit interceptor with hashes, Kafka buffering, hot PostgreSQL storage and S3 Object Lock WORM give tamper-evident 10-year retention. Gaps: asynchronous dispatch can lose events, and server-side patient-relationship policy checks are only client RBAC.
